message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge a security deposit, but it must be returned within 30 days after you move out, unless you give written notice of intent to stay.
• The deposit can only be used for unpaid rent, damages beyond normal wear & tear, or cleaning if the lease specifies it. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection checklist.
• Take photos or videos of the unit when you move in and out. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the premises in a habitable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural safety).
• Landlords must repair major problems within a reasonable time after notice. | • Report problems in writing (email or text) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent or pay for repairs and deduct the cost from your rent (but do this carefully and keep receipts). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlords cannot enter the unit without proper notice (usually 24–48 hrs) except in emergencies. | • If a landlord enters without notice, you can ask them to leave and document the incident. | | **Discrimination** | • Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a lease with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month).
• Landlords must provide a written notice of termination. | • Keep a copy of any notice you receive. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment), file a lawsuit, and obtain a court order.
• You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Attend all court hearings. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major problem, you may pay for the repair and deduct the cost from your rent, but you must give notice and keep receipts. | • Document the issue and your repair costs. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlords cannot monitor your activities inside the unit (e.g., no hidden cameras). | • If you suspect surveillance, report it to local authorities. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting** | • Texas law does not prohibit subletting, but the lease may restrict it. | • Get written permission if required. | | **Landlord’s Right to Enter** | • Landlords may enter for inspections, repairs, or to show the unit to prospective tenants, but must give reasonable notice (usually 24 hrs). | • Keep a log of entries. | | **Tenant’s Right to Organize** | • Tenants can form or join a tenant association to advocate for better conditions. | • Check local ordinances for any restrictions. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the lease thoroughly** – look for clauses on rent, security deposit, maintenance responsibilities, entry notice, and termination. 2. **Ask about habitability** – confirm that the landlord will handle major repairs. 3. **Document the unit** – take photos/videos of existing conditions. 4. **Know your notice period** – understand how much notice you need to give to move out. 5. **Check for hidden fees** – ensure any fees are disclosed and justified. ### Resources - **Texas Property Code** – the statutory framework for landlord‑tenant relations. - **Texas Commission on Human Rights** – for discrimination complaints. - **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** – for federal fair housing issues. - **Local tenant‑rights groups** – many cities have nonprofits that offer free or low‑cost legal assistance. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is for general educational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. If you have a specific legal issue, consult a qualified attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
